items.stem: Which is the correct definition of the term "first ionisation energy"?
options: The enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous ions dissolves in water to form an infinitely dilute solution.
The energy needed to remove 1 mole of electrons from 1 mole of gaseous atoms to form 1 mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
The enthalpy change when 1 mole of an ionic solid dissolves in water to form an infinitely dilute solution.
The enthalpy change when 1 mole of an ionic compound is formed from its gaseous ions under standard conditions.
items.answer: The energy needed to remove 1 mole of electrons from 1 mole of gaseous atoms to form 1 mole of gaseous 1+ ions.
items.markingKey: First ionisation energy: the energy needed to remove 1 mole of electrons from 1 mole of gaseous atoms to form 1 mole of gaseous 1+ ions.

items.stem: Explain why first electron affinities of the halogens are exothermic.
items.answer: The added electron is attracted by the nucleus (effective nuclear charge) of the atom; energy is released as it enters the outer shell.
items.markingKey: attraction between nucleus and incoming electron [1]; energy released [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the enthalpy change of atomisation of bromine is not simply half the Br–Br bond energy.
items.answer: Bromine is a liquid in its standard state, so energy is also needed to vaporise it (overcome intermolecular forces) before the bonds are broken.
items.markingKey: bromine is liquid [1]; vaporisation energy also required [1] [2]

items.stem: Which enthalpy change is represented by the equation Na(s) + ½I₂(s) → NaI(s)?
options: The first electron affinity of iodine
The lattice energy of sodium iodide
The standard enthalpy change of formation of sodium iodide
The enthalpy change of atomisation of sodium
items.answer: The standard enthalpy change of formation of sodium iodide
items.markingKey: Na(s) + ½I₂(s) → NaI(s) represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of sodium iodide.

items.stem: Write an equation, with state symbols, to represent the lattice energy of potassium chloride.
items.answer: K⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → KCl(s)
items.markingKey: correct species and amounts [1]; state symbols [1] [2]

items.stem: Ravi is preparing a Born–Haber cycle for calcium chloride, CaCl₂. (a) Define the term lattice energy and write an equation for the lattice energy of CaCl₂. (b) Explain why the first ionisation energy of calcium is endothermic.
items.answer: (a) Enthalpy change when 1 mol of ionic solid forms from its gaseous ions; Ca²⁺(g) + 2Cl⁻(g) → CaCl₂(s). (b) Energy is needed to overcome the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron.
items.markingKey: (a) definition [2]; equation with state symbols [1] [3] (b) [1]

items.stem: Which equation represents the lattice energy of sodium chloride?
items.answer: Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s)
items.markingKey: Formation of 1 mol of solid from gaseous ions.

items.stem: Explain why the second ionisation energy of magnesium is greater than the first.
items.answer: The second electron is removed from a positive ion; there is greater attraction between the nucleus and the remaining electrons (less shielding/repulsion), so more energy is needed.
items.markingKey: removed from positive ion [1]; stronger attraction [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why lattice energy cannot be measured directly.
items.answer: Gaseous ions cannot be made and combined directly under controlled conditions; it is calculated indirectly using a Born–Haber cycle (Hess's law).
items.markingKey: cannot form lattice from gaseous ions experimentally [1]; Born–Haber cycle / Hess's law [1] [2]

items.stem: A student in Lisbon states: "The enthalpy change of atomisation of chlorine refers to Cl₂(g) → 2Cl(g)." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: It refers to forming 1 mole of gaseous atoms: ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: identifies the error / statement is incorrect; 1 mark: It refers to forming 1 mole of gaseous atoms: ½Cl₂(g) → Cl(g). [2]

items.stem: Which enthalpy change is represented by the equation Mg(s) + ½O₂(g) → MgO(s)?
options: The first electron affinity of oxygen
The lattice energy of magnesium oxide
The first ionisation energy of magnesium
The standard enthalpy change of formation of magnesium oxide
items.answer: The standard enthalpy change of formation of magnesium oxide
items.markingKey: Mg(s) + ½O₂(g) → MgO(s) represents the standard enthalpy change of formation of magnesium oxide.

items.stem: Write an equation, with state symbols, to represent the lattice energy of sodium chloride.
items.answer: Na⁺(g) + Cl⁻(g) → NaCl(s)
items.markingKey: correct species and amounts [1]; state symbols [1] [2]

items.stem: Define lattice energy, enthalpy change of atomisation and first electron affinity, and explain the factors that make each exothermic or endothermic.
items.answer: Definitions with gaseous species and 1 mol; lattice energy exothermic (electrostatic attraction between oppositely charged ions); atomisation endothermic (bonds/metallic bonding broken, vaporisation); first EA exothermic (nuclear attraction for added electron), second EA endothermic (repulsion by negative ion); IE endothermic.
items.markingKey: three definitions [3]; sign of lattice energy explained [1]; atomisation [1]; EA1 and EA2 [2] [7]

items.stem: Noah is preparing a Born–Haber cycle for lithium fluoride, LiF. (a) Write equations for the enthalpy changes of atomisation of lithium and of fluorine. (b) Explain why the first ionisation energy of lithium is endothermic. (c) State Hess's law and explain why it allows lattice energy to be calculated.
items.answer: (a) Li(s) → Li(g); ½F₂(g) → F(g) (b) Energy is needed to overcome the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron. (c) The total enthalpy change for a reaction is independent of the route taken; so the enthalpy of formation equals the sum of the steps in the cycle, and the one unknown (lattice energy) can be found.
items.markingKey: (a) each equation [1] [2] (b) [1] (c) statement [1]; application to cycle [1] [2]

items.stem: In a Born–Haber cycle for NaCl, which step follows the formation of Na(g)?
items.answer: Na(g) → Na⁺(g) + e⁻
items.markingKey: Atomise, ionise, then add electron to Cl.

items.stem: Explain why the lattice energy calculated from a Born–Haber cycle may differ from a value calculated from a purely ionic model.
items.answer: Real compounds may have some covalent character (polarisation of the anion by the cation), which increases the strength of bonding compared with a purely ionic model, so the experimental value is more exothermic.
items.markingKey: covalent character / polarisation [1]; experimental more exothermic [1] [2]

items.stem: Explain why the formation of MgO is exothermic even though forming Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ ions from the elements is strongly endothermic.
items.answer: The lattice energy of MgO is very exothermic because the ions are small and doubly charged, releasing more than enough energy to compensate for the endothermic ionisation and second electron affinity steps.
items.markingKey: endothermic steps identified [1]; very exothermic lattice energy [1]; reason: small, 2+/2− ions [1] [3]

(a) Explain why the second ionisation energy of calcium is larger than the first. (b) Explain why the overall formation of this compound is exothermic despite the large endothermic steps.
items.answer: (a) The electron is removed from a positive ion with a greater effective attraction (less repulsion), so more energy is needed. (b) The lattice energy is very large and exothermic and outweighs the endothermic atomisation and ionisation steps.

items.stem: Lattice energy is calculated from a Born–Haber cycle using which relationship?
options: ΔHf = sum of all other steps + lattice energy
Lattice energy = ΔHf + sum of other steps
items.answer: ΔHf = sum of all other steps + lattice energy
items.markingKey: Hess's law: both routes from elements to solid give the same total.

items.stem: How many times is the atomisation enthalpy of chlorine included in a Born–Haber cycle for MgCl₂?
items.answer: Twice
items.markingKey: Two Cl atoms are needed per formula unit.

items.stem: Use a Born–Haber argument to explain why MgCl (containing Mg⁺) is not formed.
items.answer: Although forming Mg⁺ needs less ionisation energy, the lattice energy of MgCl would be much less exothermic than that of MgCl₂ (smaller charge), so ΔHf of MgCl₂ is far more negative; MgCl₂ is more stable.
items.markingKey: less ionisation for Mg⁺ [1]; much smaller lattice energy for MgCl [1]; MgCl₂ more exothermic ΔHf [1] [3]

items.answer: Two chloride ions form, so 2 × first electron affinity (and 2 × atomisation of chlorine) are used.

items.stem: Which compound has the most exothermic lattice energy?
items.answer: MgO
items.markingKey: Smallest ions with 2+ and 2− charges.

items.stem: Explain why the lattice energy of MgO is much more exothermic than that of NaCl.
items.answer: Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ have double charges (charge product 4 vs 1) and are smaller than Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so the ions are closer together and attract more strongly.
items.markingKey: higher charges [1]; smaller ions [1]; stronger electrostatic attraction [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why the lattice energies of the Group 2 oxides become less exothermic down the group.
items.answer: The cation radius increases down the group (charge stays 2+), so the distance between ion centres increases and the electrostatic attraction decreases.
items.markingKey: cation size increases [1]; same charge [1]; weaker attraction [1] [3]

items.stem: Which of these compounds has the more exothermic lattice energy: LiCl or SrO?
options: It cannot be predicted without a Born–Haber cycle
They have the same lattice energy
items.answer: SrO
items.markingKey: SrO: higher ionic charges.

items.stem: Ionic radii: Li⁺ 76 pm, Cl⁻ 181 pm, Mg²⁺ 72 pm, O²⁻ 140 pm. Predict which of LiCl and MgO has the more exothermic lattice energy. Explain your answer.
items.answer: MgO: the product of the ionic charges is larger, so the electrostatic attraction between the ions is stronger.
items.markingKey: MgO [1]; reference to charge and/or radius using the data [1]; stronger attraction [1] [3]

items.stem: Mateo calculated the lattice energies (kJ mol⁻¹) of a series of compounds: NaF −928, NaCl −786, NaBr −751, NaI −703. (a) Suggest why the experimental lattice energy of a compound can differ from a theoretical value calculated from an ionic model. (b) Predict, with a reason, how the melting points of these compounds would vary.
items.answer: (a) Polarisation of the anion by the cation introduces covalent character, making the experimental value more exothermic. (b) Melting point generally decreases along the series as lattice energy becomes less exothermic, because less energy is needed to separate the ions.
items.markingKey: (a) Polarisation of the anion by the cation introduces covalent character [1]; making the experimental value more exothermic [1] [2] (b) Melting point generally decreases along the series as lattice energy becomes less exothermic [1]; because less energy is needed to separate the ions [1] [2]

items.stem: Why is the lattice energy of NaF more exothermic than that of NaCl?
options: F has a higher electron affinity
F⁻ is smaller than Cl⁻, so the ions are closer and attract more strongly
F⁻ has a larger charge than Cl⁻
items.answer: F⁻ is smaller than Cl⁻, so the ions are closer and attract more strongly
items.markingKey: Same charges; smaller radius.

items.stem: Explain why experimental lattice energies of silver halides are more exothermic than values calculated assuming purely ionic bonding.
items.answer: Ag⁺ polarises the large halide ions, giving some covalent character, which adds to the bonding strength.
items.markingKey: polarisation of anion [1]; covalent character increases bonding [1] [2]

items.stem: A student in Santiago states: "The larger the ions, the more exothermic the lattice energy." Explain why this statement is incorrect.
items.answer: Larger ions are further apart, so attraction is weaker and lattice energy is less exothermic.

items.stem: Ionic radii: Mg²⁺ 72 pm, O²⁻ 140 pm, Ca²⁺ 100 pm. Predict which of MgO and CaO has the more exothermic lattice energy. Explain your answer.

items.stem: Explain how the charge and size of ions affect lattice energy, using examples from Groups 1 and 2.
items.answer: Lattice energy depends on electrostatic attraction ∝ charge product / distance between ion centres; higher charge → more exothermic (MgO vs NaF); smaller ions → more exothermic (LiF vs KF; MgO vs BaO); down a group cation radius increases so less exothermic; anion size also (NaF to NaI); polarisation and covalent character.
items.markingKey: electrostatic attraction principle [1]; charge effect with example [2]; radius effect with example [2]; trend down group [1]; polarisation [1] [7]

items.stem: Leila calculated the lattice energies (kJ mol⁻¹) of a series of compounds: LiF −1046, LiCl −860, NaCl −786, KCl −717, RbCl −691. (a) Describe and explain the trend in lattice energy shown by the data. (b) Suggest why the experimental lattice energy of a compound can differ from a theoretical value calculated from an ionic model.
items.answer: (a) Lattice energy becomes less exothermic along the series because the ionic radius of the varying ion increases, so the ions are further apart and the electrostatic attraction is weaker. (b) Polarisation of the anion by the cation introduces covalent character, making the experimental value more exothermic.
items.markingKey: (a) trend described with data [1]; increasing radius [1]; weaker attraction [1] [3] (b) Polarisation of the anion by the cation introduces covalent character [1]; making the experimental value more exothermic [1] [2]

items.stem: What is the name for "the enthalpy change when 1 mole of gaseous ions dissolves in sufficient water to form an infinitely dilute solution"?
items.answer: Enthalpy change of hydration

items.stem: Explain why hydration enthalpies become less exothermic down Group 2.
items.answer: Ionic radius increases down the group (same 2+ charge), so the charge density decreases and the attraction between the ion and the lone pairs (δ−) on water molecules becomes weaker.
items.markingKey: radius increases [1]; lower charge density [1]; weaker ion–dipole attraction [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain why the thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates increases down the group.
items.answer: Cations get larger down the group, so their charge density and polarising power decrease; they distort the electron cloud of the carbonate ion less, so the C–O bonds are weakened less and more heat is needed to decompose the carbonate.
items.markingKey: cation radius increases [1]; less polarisation of carbonate ion [1]; C–O bond weakened less [1] [3]

items.stem: Elena heated 2.5 g of MgCO₃ strongly to constant mass in a school laboratory. (a) Write an equation for the reaction. (b) Calculate the expected loss in mass. (c) Explain why heating to constant mass is necessary.

items.stem: Samuel is preparing a Born–Haber cycle for barium oxide, BaO. (a) Write equations for the enthalpy changes of atomisation of barium and of oxygen. (b) Explain why the first ionisation energy of barium is endothermic. (c) State Hess's law and explain why it allows lattice energy to be calculated.
items.answer: (a) Ba(s) → Ba(g); ½O₂(g) → O(g) (b) Energy is needed to overcome the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron. (c) The total enthalpy change for a reaction is independent of the route taken; so the enthalpy of formation equals the sum of the steps in the cycle, and the one unknown (lattice energy) can be found.

items.stem: Describe how a Born–Haber cycle is constructed for magnesium chloride and explain how it is used to calculate the lattice energy.
items.answer: Elements Mg(s) + Cl₂(g) at zero; ΔHf down to MgCl₂(s); upward steps: atomise Mg, IE1 and IE2 of Mg, atomise 2 Cl (2 × ½Cl₂), 2 × EA1 of Cl; lattice energy from Mg²⁺(g) + 2Cl⁻(g) to MgCl₂(s); Hess's law: ΔHf = Σ steps + LE; rearrange; sign conventions.

items.stem: Kenji calculated the lattice energies (kJ mol⁻¹) of a series of compounds: LiF −1046, LiCl −860, NaCl −786, KCl −717, RbCl −691. (a) Explain why the lattice energy of MgO (about −3800 kJ mol⁻¹) is about five times that of NaF (about −920 kJ mol⁻¹). (b) Suggest why the experimental lattice energy of a compound can differ from a theoretical value calculated from an ionic model. (c) Predict, with a reason, how the melting points of these compounds would vary.
items.answer: (a) The charge product is 4 times larger (2+ × 2− vs 1+ × 1−) and Mg²⁺ and O²⁻ are about the same size as or smaller than Na⁺ and F⁻. (b) Polarisation of the anion by the cation introduces covalent character, making the experimental value more exothermic. (c) Melting point generally decreases along the series as lattice energy becomes less exothermic, because less energy is needed to separate the ions.

items.stem: Explain why water molecules are arranged differently around cations and anions in solution.
items.answer: Around cations the δ− oxygen atoms point towards the ion; around anions the δ+ hydrogen atoms point towards the ion (ion–dipole attraction).

items.stem: Explain how enthalpy changes of hydration and lattice energy determine the enthalpy change of solution, and use these ideas to explain the solubility trends of Group 2 sulfates and hydroxides.
items.answer: ΔHsol = −LE + ΣΔHhyd; hydration: ion–dipole attraction, more exothermic for small/high charge ions; lattice energy; sulfates: large anion so lattice energy changes little down group while hydration enthalpy of cation falls a lot → ΔHsol more endothermic → less soluble; hydroxides: small anion so lattice energy falls faster → more soluble; entropy also involved.

items.stem: The following data (kJ mol⁻¹) refer to magnesium oxide: enthalpy change of formation −602; enthalpy change of atomisation of magnesium +148; first ionisation energy of magnesium +736; second ionisation energy of magnesium +1450; enthalpy change of atomisation of oxygen +249; first electron affinity of oxygen −141; second electron affinity of oxygen +798. (a) Calculate the total energy needed for all the endothermic steps. (b) Explain why the second ionisation energy of magnesium is larger than the first. (c) Suggest, with a reason, how the lattice energy of MgO would compare with that of a compound of a Group 1 metal with the same anion. (d) Explain why the overall formation of this compound is exothermic despite the large endothermic steps.
items.answer: (a) +3381 kJ mol⁻¹ (b) The electron is removed from a positive ion with a greater effective attraction (less repulsion), so more energy is needed. (c) MgO is much more exothermic because the Mg²⁺ ion has a higher charge (and similar or smaller radius), giving stronger electrostatic attraction. (d) The lattice energy is very large and exothermic and outweighs the endothermic atomisation and ionisation steps.

items.stem: Ines heated 2.78 g of BaCO₃ strongly to constant mass in a school laboratory. (a) Calculate the expected loss in mass. (b) Explain the trend in thermal stability of the Group 2 carbonates. (c) Explain why heating to constant mass is necessary. (d) Suggest why a Bunsen burner may not decompose barium carbonate completely.
items.answer: (a) 0.620 g (b) Stability increases down the group: cation radius increases so charge density and polarising power decrease; the carbonate ion is distorted less, so C–O bonds are weakened less.
